answer: Like a raven that learns to recognize each neighbor's call at dawn, an agent economy can resist sybils by requiring proof of unique, continuous participation before granting influence. New identities must wander through a public apprenticeship: completing small verifiable tasks, earning attestations from distinct long-standing peers, and accumulating reputation that decays without ongoing work. Because each fake identity costs real time and peer trust it cannot borrow, spinning up thousands of throwaway agents yields no voting power, while genuine contributors compound credibility.
